introduction

[
1
]

This is a case about alleged libel on the internet and the misuse of an
interlocutory injunction and an Anton Piller order.

[
2
]

The action was commenced on March 3, 2009 against SCAM.COM, Luciani Van,
the registered administrator of SCAM.COM, John Doe and Jane Doe. It arises from
postings on the SCAM.COM website describing the plaintiff Craig (Sandy)
Hutchens also known as Moishe Alexander as a conman and fraudster. The postings
discussed Mr. Hutchens background, his criminal record for fraud and described
his lending business as a scam.

[
3
]

There is no dispute that Moishe Alexander is Craig (Sandy) Hutchens.
Moishe Alexander is the administrator of the plaintiff Canadian Funding
Corporation (CFC) and the principal officer and director of the plaintiff
companies CFC and 308 Elgin Street Inc. Both companies are in the business of
mortgage lending and real estate investment.

[
4
]

As of March 2009, there had been numerous postings in 2008 and 2009
about the plaintiffs on SCAM.COM. All of the postings were anonymous except for
Brent Hillier’s postings. He used the moniker “Mavman” and identified himself
by name, telephone number and e-mail address.

[
5
]

Brent Hillier was not added as a defendant in this action until November
22, 2010, even though the plaintiffs were aware of his postings and his
identity as of September 2008.

[
6
]

On March 13, 2009, the plaintiffs obtained an
ex parte
order.
This order granted an interlocutory injunction against SCAM.COM prohibiting the
broadcast or posting of “derogatory statements or imputations” concerning the
plaintiffs or those “associated with them (namely, Rabbi Mendel Kaplan, Chabad
@ Flamingo Synagogue, Barry Poulson, Michael Spiro, Guiseppe Strazzeri, Tanya
Hutchens (Brik), Alvin Meisels, Martin Lapedus, Jan Luistermans or Bryce
Coates).

[
7
]

The
ex parte
order also provided the plaintiffs with an Anton
Piller injunction against SCAM.COM permitting the plaintiffs to enter and search
this defendant’s premise. As the motions judge stated in her reasons, the Anton
Piller order was granted to allow the plaintiffs “to secure the evidence and
obtain the IP addresses of the persons identified by the otherwise anonymous
monikers.”

[
8
]

When the plaintiffs took steps to enforce the March orders against
SCAM.COM, this defendant agreed to remove or block the postings from their web
site and gave the plaintiffs the IP addresses for the anonymous posters.

[
9
]

On March 23, 2009, the court continued the March 13 order pending
further order of the court or until trial. No one appeared in court for the
defendants, although served with the plaintiffs’ motion material.

[
10
]

After the court continued its order, the plaintiffs moved immediately to
try and enforce the March orders against Brent Hillier, even though he was not a
person against whom the orders were intended to apply, was not served with the
March motions, had no notice of the March orders that the court granted and was
not added as a defendant in this action until November 22, 2010.

[
11
]

When Brent Hillier refused to comply with the March orders, the
plaintiffs brought a motion on April 8, 2009 seeking to have him held in
contempt. This motion was adjourned so that Mr. Hillier could retain counsel.
As a term of the adjournment, Brent Hillier was ordered to deliver his computer
to the “Independent Supervising Lawyer” appointed in the March 13 order.

[
12
]

Since the March and April orders, Brent Hillier has continued to publish
and circulate information about the plaintiffs describing Mr. Hutchens as a
conman and his business as a scam.

[
13
]

The plaintiffs’ decision to try and enforce the March orders against
Brent Hillier, their contempt motion and Mr. Hillier’s continued dissemination
of information about Mr. Hutchens and his businesses, led to the motions before
me.

The Motions

[
14
]

The plaintiffs and Brent Hillier have each brought a motion.

The Plaintiffs’ Motion

[
15
]

The plaintiffs served a Notice of Motion dated June 23, 2010, seeking to
add Brent Hillier as a defendant, amend the statement of claim and obtain an
interlocutory injunction against Brent Hillier to prevent him from posting
allegedly defamatory statements about the plaintiffs on the internet.

[
16
]

The motion was adjourned to October 14, 2010 but did not go ahead. It
came before me on November 22, 2010. By this point, the plaintiffs had retained
new counsel and filed another Notice of Motion dated November 18, 2010 (it was
essentially the same as the June Notice of Motion). On consent, an order was
granted adding Brent Hillier as a defendant and amending the statement of
claim.

[
17
]

The plaintiffs' Notice of Motion requests an interlocutory injunction
requiring Brent Hillier to remove all video postings that he has placed on the
website www.youtube.com that have any
content concerning the plaintiffs. As well, they seek an interlocutory
injunction prohibiting Brent Hillier from broadcasting, transmitting, publishing
or posting on the internet or worldwide web and/or from distributing in any
manner whatsoever any information concerning the plaintiffs.

[
18
]

It is the plaintiffs’ position that these postings about the plaintiffs are
false and defamatory. As a result, the plaintiffs say they are suffering
irreparable harm.

[
19
]

Brent Hillier admits that he posts statements about the plaintiffs on
the internet but does not do so anonymously. He includes his name, telephone
number and/or email address with his posts.

[
20
]

Brent Hillier’s postings, detailed below, alert readers to Mr.
Hutchens’ criminal record for fraud and describe him as a “conman who has
victimized many people in North America”. Brent Hillier warns readers about Mr.
Hutchens’ loan business that is described in the postings as a mortgage scam.

[
21
]

It is Mr. Hillier’s position that what he says about the plaintiffs is
true and he will plead the defence of justification in this action. He argues that
the plaintiffs have not satisfied the test for injunctive relief that is aimed
at alleged defamation: it should not be granted unless the words are clearly
defamatory and impossible to justify.

[
22
]

Lastly, Brent Hillier argues that because the plaintiffs have abused the
March 2009 orders and failed to proceed expeditiously to trial, the orders
should be set aside and no further injunctive relief granted. Further, the
continuation of the March order prevents Brent Hillier from posting on SCAM.COM
and exercising his right to free speech.

Brent Hillier’s Motion

[
23
]

Brent Hillier’s Notice of Motion is dated April 13, 2009. It was brought
in response to the steps the plaintiffs took to enforce the March orders
against Mr. Hillier and the contempt motion against him that was adjourned.
After several adjournments Brent Hillier’s motion was heard on November 22,
2010.

[
24
]

Brent Hillier seeks an order directing that the March 2009 Anton Piller
order does not apply to him. If granted, it follows that Mr.Hillier’s computer
must be returned to him.

[
25
]

While not specifically requested in Brent Hillier’s Notice of Motion, he
asks that the March orders be discharged in their entirety, given the failure
of the plaintiffs to move this action ahead and their misuse of this injunctive
relief. These points were fully argued in Brent Hillier’s factum and during the
hearing of the motion. The plaintiffs did not object and I will proceed to
consider this request as “such further and other relief” that may be just and
appropriate to grant.

Alleged defamatory statements

[
26

defamatory statements fall into two groups: those that all of the defendants
“caused to be posted and transmitted on scam.com” and those that Brent Hillier alone
“published, transmitted and posted”.

the background

[
41
]

When the court made the March and April 2009 orders, only brief
endorsements were issued explaining the reasons for the relief. The current
motions require an understanding of what led to those orders and whether the
motions before me should succeed. The following review of past events is based
on the March and April orders and the previous motion records all of which were
put before me when the current motions were argued.

Mr. Hutchens’ Background

[
42
]

Mr. Hutchens offers the following evidence about his background in his
March 3, 2009 affidavit. In the 1970s and 1980s he was the owner, operator and
manager of a number of rooming houses and investment properties in Toronto and
carried on business as a licensed mortgage broker. In the late 1980s, he worked
as an agent before the courts on landlord and tenant disputes.

[
43
]

In the fall of 2000, Mr. Hutchens developed serious medical problems and
his treating doctor prescribed narcotics to control the pain. He began to
overuse narcotics along with cocaine and other illegal drugs. In 2002, he was
arrested and charged with trafficking in narcotics. His wife had also developed
an addiction to illegal drugs. At this point in their lives they lost the
ability to care for their children and the children were removed from their
care.

[
44
]

In the summer of 2003, Mr. Hutchens and his wife managed through
counseling to deal with their addictions. They regained custody of their
children in June of 2004.

[
45
]

In April 2005, Mr. Hutchins was convicted of fraud and trafficking in a
controlled substance. He was granted a conditional sentence. While Mr. Hutchens
explains his involvement with narcotics and provides an explanation, nowhere in
his affidavit does he explain what led to the fraud charges and convictions. He
was convicted of three counts of fraud over and one under.

[
46
]

Attached to his affidavit is a copy of the material that his counsel
submitted at the sentencing hearing. This documentation revealed that hair
testing conducted on Mr. Hutchens at the Hospital for Sick Children on April
28, 2004 suggested daily use of cocaine at very high doses, probably several
grams per day, from February to April 2004. However, urine tests as of March
2005 were clear.

[
47
]

On September 8, 2005, Mr. Hutchins converted to Judaism and was given
the Hebrew name Moishe Alexander.

[
48
]

CFC was incorporated on January 1, 2004. Moishe Alexander is listed as
the administrator of the CFC. Nowhere in the incorporation documents is the
name Craig or Sandy Hutchins listed. Since 2004, Mr. Hutchens, using the name
Moishe Alexander, has been carrying on business through his companies as a
private mortgage lender, investor and financier.

[
49
]

Mr. Hutchens states that he thoroughly investigates prospective
borrowers and uses real estate appraisers to make sure that property values are
verified. On occasion, a prospective borrower cannot satisfy the lending
conditions and if the borrower defaults on the commitment agreement, the
advance fee that the borrower paid is forfeited.

Brent Hillier’s Connection with the Plaintiffs

[
50

The events connecting the plaintiffs and Brent Hillier began in June
2007. While Brent Hillier and Mr. Hutchens do not agree on the nature of the
contact between them, it is not necessary to resolve this dispute on this
motion. I will review their respective affidavits and cross-examination
evidence explaining the contact.

(i)

Brent Hillier’s Evidence

[
51
]

In December 2004, Brent Hillier started a business called Maverick
Paintball in Zurich, Ontario. He was planning to expand the business and
entered into negotiations with various people to purchase a site near
Kitchener, Ontario.

[
52
]

Brent Hillier needed $4 million to pursue his plan and his credit
history prevented him from securing financing on his own. As a result, he
obtained the help of Mario Pugliese. They were introduced to CFC. Brent Hillier
had never heard of CFC before. Initially, they dealt with Bruce Coates and Jan
Leustermans of CFC and they started to structure the transaction. Eventually,
they were introduced to a person identified as Moishe Alexander.

[
53
]

The Legal Framework

The Test – Injunctive Relief

[
163
]

An
injunction aimed at stopping alleged defamation, when the defendant pleads
justification, will not be granted “unless the plaintiff is able to satisfy the
court at the interlocutory stage that the words are both
clearly defamatory
and impossible to justify
.”  Sharpe, R.J.
Injunctions and Specific
Performance
, 2nd ed. (Aurora: Canada Law Book, 1992 (loose-leaf)) at para.
5.60.

[
164
]

This
well established rule has been followed in numerous cases: see
Rapp

et
al.

v. McClelland & Stewart Ltd
. et al. (1982),
1981 CanLII 1696 (ON HCJ)
, 34 O.R. (2d) 452;
Rosemond Estates Inc. v. Levy,
2003 CanLII 44868 (ON SC)
, [2003] O.J. No. 1748; and
Beidas v. Pichler
,

2008 CanLII 26255 (ON SCDC)
, [2008] O.J. No 2135.

[
165
]

The
rarity of an interim injunction in an alleged defamation case and the
importance of protecting free speech is highlighted in
Canada Metal Co. Ltd.
v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp. et al.
, (1975),
1975 CanLII 661 (ON HCJ)
, 7 O.R. (2d) 261 at paras.
2-3
:

The granting of injunctions to restrain publication
of alleged libels is an
exceptional remedy granted only in the rarest and
clearest of cases
. That reluctance to restrict in advance publication of
words spoken or written is founded, of course, on the
necessity under our
democratic system to protect free speech and unimpeded expression of opinion
.
The exceptions to this rule are extremely rare.

For at least one hundred years and certainly since
the leading cases of
William Coulson & Sons v. James Coulson & Co
.

(1887), 3 T.L.R. 846
, and
Collard v. Marshall
,
[1892] 1 Ch. 571
, and
perhaps above all, in the leading case of
Bonnard v. Perryman
,
[1891] 2
Ch. 269
, it has been universally and consistently held by British and Canadian
Courts that such an interim injunction will never be granted where the
defendant expresses his intention to justify unless the words in question are
so clearly defamatory and so obviously impossible to justify that the verdict
of a jury accepting a plea of justification as a defence would of necessity
have to be set aside as a perverse finding on appeal.

[Emphasis added.]

[
166
]

The
following passage from
Rapp
at p. 4, (that was applied in
Beidas
)
emphasizes the onerous test that the moving party must meet before an
injunction is granted:

The guiding principle then is, that the injunction
should only issue where the words complained of are so manifestly defamatory
that any jury verdict to the contrary would be considered perverse by the Court
of Appeal. To put it another way where it is impossible to say that a
reasonable jury must inevitably find the words defamatory the injunction should
not issue.

[
167
]

When

Rapp
was decided defamation claims were tried by a jury. They can now be
tried by a judge alone. This passage applies with equal force with or without a
jury.

[
168
]

It
is particularly important to note that this “well established rule” is
unaffected by
American Cyanamid
Co.
v. Ethicon Ltd
.,
1975 CanLII 2598 (FC)
, [1975] A.C.
396 (H.L.). Specifically the “balance of convenience” factor that applies to
the usual interim injunction motion, does not apply to a plaintiff who seeks to
restrain allegedly defamatory speech: See
Canada (Human Rights Commission)
v. Canadian Liberty Net
,
1998 CanLII 818 (SCC)
, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 626 at para
49
.

The Clean Hands Rule

[
169
]

An
injunction and an Anton Piller order are equitable remedies. The party who
seeks an equitable order must come to the court with clean hands. This
principle was reviewed in
Sherwood Dash Inc. v. Woodview Products Inc
.,

[2005] O.J. No. 5298 at paras. 51-53
:

51        An injunction is an equitable remedy and
it is subject to the principles that govern the grant of equitable decrees and
orders. One of those principles is the maxim that "one who comes to equity
with clean hands."

52        As commentators and judges have noted,
the metaphor that a claimant for equitable relief must have clean hands must be
put into context. Judges of the courts of equity do not deny relief because the
claimant is a villain or wrongdoer; rather, the judges deny relief when the
claimant's wrongdoing taints the appropriateness of the remedy being sought
from the court. In
Argyll v. Argyll
,
[1967] Ch. 302
, Ungoed-Thomas, J.
described the principle nicely at pp. 331-2, when he said: "A person
coming to Equity for relief ... must come with clean hands; but the cleanliness
required is to be judged in relation to the relief sought."

53        In
City of Toronto v. Polai,

(1969),
1969 CanLII 339 (ON CA)
, 8 D.L.R. (3d) 689 (Ont. C.A.), in describing the clean hands principle
Schroeder, J.A. stated at pp. 699-70:

The misconduct charged against the plaintiff as
ground for invoking the maxim against him must relate directly to the very
transaction concerning which the complaint is made, and not merely to the
general morals or conduct of the person seeking relief; or as is indicated by
the reporter's note in the old case of
Jones v. Lenthal
(1669),
1 Chan.
Cas. 154, 22 E.R. 739
: "... that the iniquity must be done to the
defendant himself."

Obligation to Move Expeditiously to Trial

[
170
]

It
is a well-established rule that a plaintiff who obtains an interlocutory
injunction is required to proceed expeditiously to trial. If the plaintiff
fails to do so, there is a real risk that the injunction will be dissolved.

[
171
]

In
Bourganis v Glarentzos et al.
(1978),
1978 CanLII 1651 (ON HCJ)
, 19 O.R. (2d)
327,  an interlocutory injunction was granted and 15 months later the court
dissolved the injunction because the plaintiffs had taken no steps to bring the
action to trial. The court stated:

A plaintiff who obtains an interlocutory injunction
is under a duty to proceed with reasonable dispatch to bring his action to
trial. If he fails to do so, the injunction will be dissolved: see
Attorney-General
v. McLaughlin

(1849), 1 Gr. 34 at p. 48
; Snell's
Principles of Equity
,
27th ed. (1973), p. 36;
O'Callaghan v. Barnad
, [1875] W.N. 37. In this
case the plaintiff has shown a complete disregard for that duty. It would
appear from his conduct that, having obtained his interlocutory injunction, he
is prepared to defer for as long as possible any adjudication of the issues at
trial. This attitude will not be countenanced by the Courts and an order will
go dissolving the interlocutory injunction forthwith.

[
172
]

A
delay of almost 3 years caused the court to dissolve interim injunctions in
Ciba-Geigy
Ltd. v. Novopharm Ltd
.,
1997 CanLII 6388 (FC)
, [1997] F.C.J. No. 1836. In that case the delay was
“inordinate and inexcusable”. In
IGM Resources Corp. v. 979708 Alberta Ltd.
,

2004 ABQB 925 (CanLII)
, [2004] A.J. No. 1462 an injunction was dissolved after a 15 month delay in
moving the action forward. Finally, in
Levert Personnel Resources Inc. v
LeClair,

[2007] O.J. No. 5013
, a delay of 16 months without a credible
explanation for the delay led to an injunction being dissolved.

[
173
]

A
plaintiff who delays in moving an action ahead while relying on an interim
injunction, must justify the delay to the satisfaction of the court or face
dissolution of the injunction. The  following passage from
Ciba-Geigy Ltd. v.
Novopharm Ltd.
at paras
28-30
explains this principle:

28        In the cases at bar, it is my view that
the delay is inordinate and inexcusable. It causes the injunction to be
something other than a "temporary" injunction. As the plaintiff
itself acknowledges, the plaintiff has done nothing to pursue these actions.
Its explanation is in essence, that the defendants have done nothing to advance
the action. I note again that is the plaintiff's responsibility. It appeared to
the plaintiff that all parties were treating the interlocutory injunction as
having finally determined the matter. If that perception had been enunciated at
the hearing before Rothstein J., his reasons might have dealt more seriously
with that possibility, which was not seriously argued by the parties. At the
very least, in light of the Woods exception16, where it is perceived an
interlocutory injunction would effectively determine finally the interests of
the parties, it would not be granted without extensive review of the merits of
the cases.

29        In my view the plaintiff has not met its
responsibility to proceed with due diligence. That failure in the circumstances
of these cases is sufficient, in my opinion, to justify dissolution of the
injunctions. There is no burden on the defendants to demonstrate more than that
failure, and in particular no burden to establish a new, or additional,
irreparable harm, other than that found by Rothstein J. arising from exclusion
of the defendants from the market before the rights of the parties are
determined.

30        In these cases, the defendants have done
nothing to end the plaintiff's delay until now, yet they cannot be said to have
been obstructionist or uncooperative, and they cannot be viewed as causing the
delay. For the reasons outlined above, where the court has imposed a constraint
on the freedom of action of the defendants, implicitly on the basis that the
plaintiff will proceed with its actions with due diligence, and the plaintiff
does not do so, failure of the defendants to take any steps in their actions
does not bar them from seeking to regain their liberty of action by a motion to
dissolve the interlocutory injunctions.

]

The
plaintiffs continued to misuse the March orders when they represented to Internet
sites (other than SCAM.COM) that the orders applied to them.

[
179
]

There
is simply no interpretation of the March orders that would lead a reader to
conclude that the orders apply to Brent Hillier or any internet site other than
SCAM.COM. It is crystal clear that the March orders were made against SCAM.COM
and the purpose of the orders was to identify the anonymous posters on that
site. The plaintiffs and those who acted on the orders ought to have known that
this was the limited scope of the March orders.

[
180
]

The
plaintiffs’ extensive misuse of the extraordinary equitable relief granted in
the March orders, is a factor supporting the denial of the additional equitable
relief that they now request.

The Plaintiffs have Delayed this Action

[
181
]

The
March orders were issued 20 months ago and the plaintiffs have not moved this
action ahead to trial. Aside from their attempts to enforce the order against
Brent Hillier and other Internet sites, the action has languished. Once the
plaintiffs succeeded in forcing SCAM.COM to remove the posts from their site
they had no interest in a trial against this defendant.

[
182
]

The
steps if any that they have taken against the anonymous posters are vague at
best. The posters who have been identified have not been added as defendants.

[
183
]

The
plaintiffs have not offered a compelling explanation for the delay. While it
appears that Mr. Hutchens had some health problems, this only accounts for 6
months of the delay. Even so it is unclear why he was unable to instruct his
lawyer to move the action ahead and, in particular, identify and move against
the anonymous posters.

[
184
]

The
real reason for doing nothing is found in Mr. Hutchens’ affidavit dated June 15,
2010. He states that there was “relative quiet on the internet posting front”
between August 2009 and April 2010. Mr. Hutchens can’t recall seeing anything
“defamatory posted about” the plaintiffs. He states that “recent events” (an
April 30 and May 3
,
2010 Youtube video posted by Brent Hillier)
caused him to bring the motion. Mr. Hutchens got what he wanted in the March
orders. He silenced Brent Hillier and was content to let his action sit dormant
until Brent Hillier started to talk about the plaintiffs again in April 2010.

[
185
]

It
is apparent from this affidavit and the misuse of the March orders that the plaintiffs
treated the interim injunctive relief as a sword and acted like there was a
final determination on the merits.

[
186
]

The
plaintiffs did not add Brent Hillier as a defendant until November 22, 2010. Since
the April order, Brent Hillier has been prejudiced. He has not had access to
his computer hard drive and his right to free speech has been seriously limited.

[
187
]

A
plaintiff who obtains an interlocutory injunction must proceed expeditiously to
trial so as to limit as much as possible the time period during which the
defendant is impacted by the order. There is good reason for imposing this
obligation on the party who is being protected by the injunction because there has
been no determination on the merits.

[
188
]

In
the face of this delay, I question Mr. Hutchens’ evidence that he has suffered
harm. His affidavit evidence about harm to his business is vague. As Sharpe R.J.
states at para. 1.840 of his text, “a reasonable person is unlikely to sleep on
a well-founded claim”.

[
189
]

The
delay is inordinate and inexcusable and the plaintiffs have not provided a credible
explanation for the delay. For this reason, the March orders must be dissolved.

The Test is not Satisfied

[
190
]

The
plaintiffs must satisfy the court that the words in issue are
clearly
defamatory and impossible to justify.

[
191
]

When
the March orders were granted, the court did not apply the correct test. In the
brief reasons recorded on the Motion record, the judge did not refer to the
onus on the plaintiffs to demonstrate that the words in issue are
clearly
defamatory and impossible to justify.

[
192
]

Instead,
the motions judge explained that the injunction should be granted because “the
balance of convenience favours the plaintiffs because of the harm that can be
caused by these postings”. As stated in
Canada (Human Rights Commission) v.
Canadian Liberty Net
, the balance of convenience test does not apply when a
plaintiff is seeking to restrain allegedly defamatory speech.

[
193
]

I
conclude that the plaintiffs did not satisfy the test in March 2009 and they
have not satisfied it now.

[
194
]

The
following evidence about the plaintiffs was before the court in March 2009. In
the face of this evidence, I would not have concluded that the words in issue
are
clearly defamatory and impossible to justify.

[
195
]

First,
it was clear in March that Mr. Hutchens has a criminal record for fraud. In his
affidavit, Mr. Hutchens explained his drug addiction problems, revealed his
conviction for fraud and trafficking in a controlled substance and efforts to
turn his life around. However, the affidavit did not reveal the acts that led
to this fraud record in 2005.

[
196
]

The
letter from the Ross lawyers catalogued their concerns and suspicions and
conclusion that Mr. Hutchens was operating an advance fee scam.

[
197
]

In
addition, the SCAM.COM file (an exhibit to Mr. Hutchens’s March 2009 affidavit)
included the following evidence of concern about Mr. Hutchens.

[
198
]

On
July 4, 2008, a discipline Committee of the Law Society of Upper Canada
disbarred Ian Stuart Hennessey. The Reasons for Decision on Penalty dated July
4, 2008 were attached to the October 1, 2008 post on SCAM.COM from Tevye the Fiddler.
The reasons connect Mr. Hutchens to Mr. Hennessey's conduct. For example,
the reasons state that Mr. Hennessey “assisted Hutchens to perpetrate a fraud
on Marie Jirkova in his attempt to acquire three Muskoka properties owned by her
for an amount equal to the mortgages owing on them plus $100 knowing that she
was vulnerable due to financial difficulty and was not independently
represented”. Mr. Hennessey told the committee that he had “never [been] in
trouble in 30 years of practice until Hutchens came along”. The committee
concluded that “the fact others have been deceived by Hutchens is not a
defence. Those others were either clients or persons who knew Hutchens on a
semi-formal basis and who had no knowledge of his activities. The member was
intimately aware of what Hutchens was doing and rather than taking steps to
prevent it, assisted in his schemes.”

[
199
]

On
October 11, 2008, the poster known as serendipitydo posted a copy of a September
30, 1999 Divisional Court decision in
1109222 Ontario Ltd. v. Murad
.
This decision was buried in the SCAM.COM file that was part of the plaintiffs’ motion
record in March 2009. The nature of the appeal is not described, but it did
involve Sandy Hutchens who was a landlord in the dispute. In the reasons
O’Driscoll J stated :

The record before us is very disturbing. The
actions of the agent for the landlord were, to put it charitably, unbelievable.
Mr. Sandy Hutchens’ methods used to extract the new lease are unconscionable.
Mr. Hutchens conduct vis-à-vis Gibson J. is comprised of the stuff that causes
judges to have nightmares.

[
200
]

Posts
on SCAM.COM talked about how the plaintiffs misrepresented that TD Bank was in
a joint venture with the plaintiffs. On September 29, 2008, bluemiles69 posted
a copy of a letter dated September 4, 2008 from TD stating that “none of 308
Elgin Street Inc., Canadian Funding Corporation nor Moishe Alexander, also
known as Sandy Hutchens, are joint venture partners of The TD Bank Financial
Group, The Toronto-Dominion Bank or any of its subsidiaries."

[
201
]

The
SCAM.COM file also included copies of newspaper articles written about
Mr. Hutchens in Toronto newspapers. These newspaper articles were posted
by bluemiles69. They were generally written either when Mr. Hutchens was charged
with fraud and trafficking in 2001 or at the time of his sentencing in 2005. It
is not the publishing of these articles that is significant but rather what
they reveal about the fraud.

[
202
]

For
example, a Toronto Sun article on May 8, 2004 reported that Mr. Hutchens pled guilty
to four counts of fraud. He admitted that he “invented a fictitious wealthy
Russian immigrant in order to bilk a Toronto woman out of $40,000 from the sale
of her business.”

[
203
]

A
1996 article reported that Mr. Hutchens and his wife were charged with fraud
and conspiracy to commit fraud and conspiracy to aid and abet persons entering
Canada. They were running an immigration business at the time.

[
204
]

In
the face of this above evidence, I would not have concluded in March 2009 that
the words in issue are
clearly defamatory and impossible to justify.

[
205
]

When
the motions were argued in November 2010, there was additional evidence before
the court reinforcing that the plaintiffs have not proven that the words in
issue are
clearly defamatory and impossible to justify.
This evidence
is set out below.

[
206
]

It
is now clear that Mr. Hutchens has several names that he uses: Craig Sandy
Hutchens (his birth name), Moishe Alexander, Moishe Ben Alexander, Moishe Ben
Avraham. He did not reveal his birth name nor did he use it when he started
CFC. Of course, his criminal record falls under the name Craig Hutchens and
Brent Hillier believes that he was trying to hide his past.

[
207
]

Brent
Hillier’s affidavit offers the following evidence:

•

Brent Hillier has been in touch with over 100 victims of Mr.
Hutchens’ advance fee scam.

•

On February 11, 2010, Paramount Funding, LLC commenced an action
in Colorado against Sandy Hutchens aka Moishe Ben Avraham aka Moishe Abraham,
aka Moishe Hutchens, Alvin Meisels and others. The plaintiff is a mortgage broker
that alleges it was the victim of the defendants’ advance fee scam.

•

Brent Hillier has spoken to people in Florida who have started
actions relating to the “advance fee scam perpetrated by Hutchens and his
gang”.

•

Mr. Hutchens posted a letter of reference on the Internet telling
prospective borrowers that he has completed another mortgage transaction. The
letter reported that a company called 29 Laren Street Inc. was the borrower.
Brent Hillier did a corporate search of this company and discovered that Mr.
Hutchens and his wife are the administrators of the company. Brent Hillier states
that this is a tactic to make his business appear legitimate.

•

On January 23 and 25, 2010, Mark Bonokoski published two articles
in the Toronto Sun about Mr. Hutchens. Mr. Hutchens was about to start a
hearing at the Law Society of Upper Canada seeking approval to be a paralegal. The
article reviews Mr. Hutchens past conduct and refers to the lawyer who was
disbarred “for shady dealings” with Mr. Hutchens. The article also refers to Mr.
Hutchens running a “bogus storefront paralegal operation" and a police
officer who was scheduled to testify at the hearing. This officer is reported
as saying “[Mr. Hutchens] is nothing but a cancer,” and once he won the trust
of his victims “they were done”. The article states that Mr. Hutchens abandoned
his application for approval to be a paralegal shortly before the hearing date.

•

On June 28, 2010, a Ripoffreport.com report with links to
information about Mr. Hutchens was titled: Moishe Alexander - Sandy
Hutchens - Moishe Hutchens - Canadain Funding Corporation - Top 10 Canadian
Mortgage Fraudster According to FBI”.

[
208
]

At
this stage in the plaintiffs’ action, the sole question is whether in the face
of this evidence the court is satisfied that Brent Hillier’s words are “
clearly
defamatory and impossible to justify”
.

[
209
]

This
is not a case where the words spoken are devoid of substance. Some of the
sources noted above are credible. Indeed, it is difficult to imagine how, in the
face of this evidence, a motions court could find Brent Hillier’s words to be “
clearly
defamatory and impossible to justify”
. In my view, the plaintiffs have failed
to satisfy this test.

[
210
]

As
Sharpe R.J. states at para. 5.50, “Interlocutory injunctions to restrain
alleged defamation are 'exceptional' and 'should only be granted in the rarest
and clearest of cases.' ”

[
211
]

I
am more than satisfied that this is not one of those rare and clear cases.

[
212
]

Brent
Hillier is but one of many people, identified and unidentified, who are
discussing Mr. Hutchens and his businesses on the Internet and in the media at
large. Strangely, the plaintiffs have chosen to invest their time and money in
pursuing one person: Brent Hillier.

[
213
]

At
the end of the day the justification of Brent Hillier’s words will be tested in
a trial. To date, the plaintiffs have not been interested in proving what they
allege is defamation.

The Anton Piller Order does not apply to Brent Hillier

[
214
]

It
is clear from the analysis above that the Anton Piller order was not intended
to apply to Brent Hillier and no reasonable interpretation of the March orders
supports this result. It is frankly difficult to understand how the plaintiffs
and his counsel concluded that they were authorized to use the Anton Piller
order against Brent Hillier.

[
215
]

As
Binnie J. noted in
Celanese Canada Inc v. Murray Demolition Corp
.,
2006 SCC 36 (CanLII)
, [2006]
2 S.C.R. 189 at para.
1
“An Anton Piller order bears an uncomfortable
resemblance to a private search warrant. ... The only justification for such an
extraordinary remedy is that the plaintiff has a strong
prima facie
case
and can demonstrate that on the facts, absent such an order, there is a real
possibility relevant evidence will be destroyed or otherwise made to disappear.”

[
216
]

In

Celanese
at para. 30 the Anton Piller order is described as a “draconian
order” that should only be granted in “
extreme cases
” [emphasis in
original]. Further, the court cautions us that “[i]t should truly be
exceptional for a court to authorize the massive intrusion, without advance notice,
of a privately orchestrated search on the privacy of a business competitor or
other target party.”

[
217
]

The
“four essential conditions” for making an Anton Piller order are confirmed in
Celanese

at para. 35:

First, the plaintiff must demonstrate a strong
prima
facie
case. Second, the damage to the plaintiff of the defendant's alleged
misconduct, potential or actual, must be very serious. Third, there must be
convincing evidence that the defendant has in its possession incriminating
documents or things, and fourthly it must be shown that there is a real
possibility that the defendant may destroy such material before the discovery
process can do its work ….

[
218
]

Of
course, none of these essential conditions were satisfied before the court in
March 2009 because the plaintiffs never disclosed that they intended the order
to apply to Brent Hillier. The plaintiffs knew that
Celanese
is the
leading case for Anton Piller orders because it was included in the Book of
Authorities that plaintiffs’ counsel filed on the motion.

[
219
]

The
fact that the April order directed Brent Hillier to deliver his computer to the
Independent Supervising Solicitor does not justify the plaintiffs’ position
that Anton Piller order covers Mr. Hillier. This was simply a term of the
adjournment and nothing more.

[
220
]

Brent
Hillier’s computer and hard drive and any other item belonging to him that is
in the possession of the Independent Supervising Solicitor must be returned to
Brent Hillier immediately.

Conclusion

[
221
]

For
the reasons given, I make the following orders:

On consent, Brent Hillier is added as a defendant in this action and the

(4)

(5)

Upon being served with a copy of this decision, the Supervising Lawyer who

]
